review_verdict: Owner-provided independent NotebookLM verdict: all 35/35 entries PASS, no required/optional corrections or duplicates; no topic-linked lessons authorized; read-only reference only.

entries.title: look after
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Care for a person, animal or thing for a period of time.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: look after + object; the object normally follows the whole expression: look after her, not look her after.
entries.independent_illustration: When their neighbours travelled, Salma looked after their two rabbits.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: This describes providing care, not just briefly looking at the rabbits; it differs from look up, which can mean search for information (existing REF-PHR-01).
entries.watch_out_or_limits: In some contexts, look after also means deal with a task. Do not claim it always means childcare.
entries.learner_self_check: Can I name who or what receives care after the two-word verb?

entries.title: put off
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Postpone an activity or event to a later time.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: put off + noun or put + pronoun + off: put off the trip / put it off. The postponement sense is separable.
entries.independent_illustration: The club put off its outdoor meeting because a storm was forecast.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The meeting is delayed, not necessarily cancelled; cancel would mean it will not take place as planned.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Put someone off can instead mean discourage or repel them; surrounding context determines the sense. Not put off it for this object-pronoun pattern.
entries.learner_self_check: Can I replace the event with it and place it correctly?

entries.title: carry on
entries.register_or_mode: neutral; especially common in British English
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Continue an activity already in progress.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: carry on + -ing or carry on with + noun: carry on drawing / carry on with the project.
entries.independent_illustration: Although the library was noisy, the volunteers carried on sorting donated books.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The work continues despite the interruption; this is different from starting a fresh task.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Carry on has other meanings, including behave in an excited or disorderly way; avoid forcing a continuation reading in every context.
entries.learner_self_check: Does my sentence say what continues, and have I used -ing or with appropriately?

entries.title: figure out
entries.register_or_mode: neutral to informal, frequent in speech
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Understand something or find a solution after thinking.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: figure out + noun or figure + pronoun + out: figure out the route / figure it out.
entries.independent_illustration: After comparing the two maps, Jun finally figured out which path led to the station.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Figure out suggests reaching an understanding or answer, not simply seeing the information.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: In formal writing, determine, understand or solve may sometimes suit the context better; the phrasal verb is not a universal synonym for all three.
entries.learner_self_check: Does the expression identify the problem or information understood, and is a pronoun placed between the verb and particle?

entries.title: take up
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Begin a hobby or regular activity.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: take up + activity/noun: take up painting / take up a new sport. With a pronoun: take it up.
entries.independent_illustration: Last winter, Rosa took up birdwatching and started keeping a notebook of sightings.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: This says a new interest started; carry on describes continuing an existing activity.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Take up can also mean occupy time/space or accept an offer or challenge. The hobby sense is not appropriate in all sentences.
entries.learner_self_check: Does my example introduce a new regular interest, rather than a task that was already underway?

entries.title: make a decision
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Choose between possible actions after considering options.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: make + a decision; often make a decision about/on something or decide to + verb.
entries.independent_illustration: After visiting both clubs, An decided to join the robotics club; she made the decision on Friday.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Make a decision is the idiomatic verb–noun partnership; do a decision is not ordinary standard usage.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Decide is often simpler and more natural than a long noun phrase. The exact preposition depends on construction.
entries.learner_self_check: Can I rewrite my phrase naturally with the verb decide without changing meaning?

entries.title: pay attention to
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Concentrate on information, a person or an activity.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: pay attention to + noun/-ing; here to is a preposition: pay attention to the signs / to how the speaker changes topic.
entries.independent_illustration: Before crossing the trail bridge, the hikers paid attention to the warning sign.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The words form a common partnership; give attention to occurs but differs in style and often emphasis.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Do not use to + base verb just because the expression contains to. Other constructions, such as draw attention to, are separate collocations.
entries.learner_self_check: Is the thing I should notice clearly expressed after to?

entries.title: take responsibility for
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Accept a duty or acknowledge responsibility for an action or outcome.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: take responsibility for + noun/-ing.
entries.independent_illustration: After the exhibition, the class committee took responsibility for returning the borrowed tables.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: This expression focuses on accepting duty; be responsible for can describe an existing duty without highlighting the act of accepting it.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Responsibility can involve accountability or a practical assigned task. The expression does not imply someone is legally at fault.
entries.learner_self_check: Have I stated what responsibility is accepted, not just who is responsible?

entries.title: do research on/into
entries.register_or_mode: neutral; conduct research is often more formal
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Investigate a question by gathering and examining information.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: do research on/into + topic; research is usually uncountable in this general meaning.
entries.independent_illustration: For the school exhibition, the group did research on how local trees survive long dry periods.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Conduct research is an alternative, especially in academic prose; make a research is not idiomatic for the general activity.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: A study or a research project can name one particular investigation; this does not make general research routinely countable.
entries.learner_self_check: Can I replace do research with investigate while keeping the intended meaning?

entries.title: draw a conclusion
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Reach a reasoned judgement from available information or evidence.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: draw a conclusion from + evidence or plural draw conclusions.
entries.independent_illustration: The seedlings near the window grew taller; the class drew a cautious conclusion that light might have played a role.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The expression highlights an inference from observations rather than a mere preference.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: An observation alone may not establish causation. Reach a conclusion is also natural; do not force draw in every register.
entries.learner_self_check: Have I named the evidence and avoided a stronger conclusion than it supports?

entries.title: decide / decision / decisive
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Recognize related word forms without treating them as interchangeable.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: Verb decide (to do); noun decision (about/on); adjective decisive = effective in settling a question or showing determination, depending on context.
entries.independent_illustration: The team had to decide by noon. Their decision was final. A decisive vote ended the debate.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Decision names the choice; decisive describes an action, factor or person rather than being a noun form of decide.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: A decided change or a decisive change is not always the same thing; spelling relation does not guarantee identical meaning.
entries.learner_self_check: Can I mark the verb, noun and adjective in the three sentences?

entries.title: succeed / success / successful
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Express achievement using verb, noun and adjective patterns.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: Verb succeed in + -ing; noun success; adjective successful (in/at something).
entries.independent_illustration: Linh succeeded in repairing the bicycle. The repair was a success, and her first test ride was successful.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The verb focuses on achieving an aim; the noun names the achievement or a successful event; the adjective describes its result.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Success can be countable or uncountable according to meaning; succeed to can have a different formal meaning involving inheriting a position/title.
entries.learner_self_check: After succeeded in, did I use a noun or an -ing form?

entries.title: explain / explanation / explanatory
entries.register_or_mode: neutral; explanatory is often more academic
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Distinguish an act of explaining from an explanation and something that helps explain.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: Verb explain + something (to someone); noun an explanation (of/for something); adjective explanatory before a noun.
entries.independent_illustration: The guide explained the symbols to the visitors. Her explanation was clear, and the explanatory diagram was easy to follow.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Explain is a verb; explanation names the information or act; explanatory describes a diagram, note or method.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: In standard English, say explain the rule to me, not explain me the rule. Explanatory is not the ordinary past participle of the verb.
entries.learner_self_check: Can I change explain the symbols into give an explanation of the symbols naturally?

entries.title: differ / difference / different
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Compare things using related verb, noun and adjective forms.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: Verb differ from; noun a difference between; adjective different from (other prepositions also occur by variety/context).
entries.independent_illustration: The two routes differ in length. One difference between them is the number of stairs. They are also different in cost.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Differ reports variation as a verb; difference names a contrast; different describes something as unlike another.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Prepositions vary by dialect and construction (different from/to/than). Do not mark every regional alternative as inherently wrong.
entries.learner_self_check: Does my sentence need a verb, a noun, or an adjective in the gap?

entries.title: create / creation / creative
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Distinguish producing something from the product/process and the quality of originality.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: Verb create + object; noun creation (the act or something made); adjective creative (showing imagination or inventiveness).
entries.independent_illustration: The students created a small maze. Their creation entertained visitors, and the creative design used recycled boxes.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: A created object is not automatically creative; the adjective says something about originality or invention.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Creative can also describe a person or profession; it is not a universal replacement for created.
entries.learner_self_check: Am I describing what was made or how imaginative it is?

entries.title: say vs tell
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Choose the reporting verb based on whether the message or listener is emphasized.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: say + something / say something to + person; tell + person + something in the common reporting pattern.
entries.independent_illustration: Noor said that the hall was closed. She told her brother the news.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Said can introduce the message without a direct-person object; told commonly names who received the information.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Expressions such as tell the truth and say hello have their own patterns. Do not generalize that tell must always take a person immediately after it.
entries.learner_self_check: If I name the listener after said, do I need to in this construction?

entries.title: job vs work
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Distinguish a specific role/task from the broader activity of working.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: A job is often countable (two part-time jobs); work meaning employment or activity is usually uncountable (a lot of work).
entries.independent_illustration: Eva found a weekend job at a museum. She enjoys the work but has a lot of work to finish before Friday.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Job may identify a position or task; work can describe the activity or responsibilities rather than one position.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Works can be countable in special senses (artworks, engineering works); a work exists in certain contexts. Do not claim work is never countable.
entries.learner_self_check: Am I referring to one position/task or work as an amount of activity?

entries.title: fun vs funny
entries.register_or_mode: everyday; fun as an adjective is common informally
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Choose fun for enjoyment and funny for humour or something odd.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: have fun, a fun activity (common informal adjective); a funny story = amusing or strange, depending on context.
entries.independent_illustration: The science trail was fun, and the guide told a funny story about a runaway robot.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Enjoyment need not involve laughter; a joke can be funny even if an event is not generally enjoyable.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Funny can mean suspicious or unusual, not only humorous. Calling a serious incident funny may communicate the wrong tone.
entries.learner_self_check: Do I mean “enjoyable”, “amusing” or “strange”?

entries.title: advice vs advise
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Distinguish the noun for guidance from the verb for giving guidance.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: Noun advice (normally uncountable: some advice, a piece of advice); verb advise + person + to-infinitive.
entries.independent_illustration: The coach gave Sam useful advice. She advised him to rest before the next race.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The noun names guidance; the verb describes the action of recommending something.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Spelling differs (-ce vs -se) and the usual pronunciations differ in the final sound. Do not write an advice for a single ordinary suggestion.
entries.learner_self_check: Can I replace the word with “guidance” (noun) or “recommend” (verb)?

entries.title: actually vs currently
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Separate a correction or reality marker (actually) from a present-time marker (currently).
entries.pattern_or_procedure: actually often means in fact; currently means at present, often with a situation that may change.
entries.independent_illustration: I thought the art room was on the second floor, but it is actually on the first. It is currently closed for repairs.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The first adverb corrects a belief; the second reports the room's present status.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Actually can also soften or introduce conversational remarks, not always contradiction. Do not use it as a synonym for now.
entries.learner_self_check: Am I correcting a fact or telling the reader what is true at this time?

entries.title: once in a blue moon
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Something happens very rarely.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: Often used as an adverbial phrase: I go there once in a blue moon.
entries.independent_illustration: Our neighbourhood holds a night-time telescope event only once in a blue moon.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: It communicates rarity figuratively rather than a literal lunar schedule.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: It is not a mathematically fixed frequency or substitute for a measured interval. The existing Frequency Expressions ladder remains qualitative.
entries.learner_self_check: Could I replace it with very rarely without changing the intended meaning?

entries.title: a piece of cake
entries.meaning_or_strategy: A task is very easy for the speaker in the given situation.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: something is/was a piece of cake.
entries.independent_illustration: After practising the route all week, finding the museum was a piece of cake for Theo.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The idiom evaluates difficulty, not food or actual cake.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: It is informal and subjective; calling someone's difficult experience a piece of cake may sound dismissive.
entries.learner_self_check: Would very easy fit the sentence, and is an informal idiom suitable for the reader?

entries.title: hit the books
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Start studying seriously or devote concentrated time to studying.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: hit the books; often a brief statement of intention: I need to hit the books.
entries.independent_illustration: With the astronomy quiz next week, Dara decided to hit the books after dinner.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The phrase means study, not physically strike printed books.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: It is casual; it may not suit a formal study report or academic essay.
entries.learner_self_check: Is the context about serious study rather than a literal action?

entries.title: the last straw
entries.meaning_or_strategy: The final additional problem that makes a difficult situation intolerable.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: the last straw or the final straw, often with a preceding series of difficulties.
entries.independent_illustration: Three printers had broken that week. When the last working printer jammed, it was the last straw for the team.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The final jam is not the only problem; it pushes a build-up of frustrations past a limit.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Do not use it for any single minor inconvenience with no implied accumulation, unless exaggeration is deliberate.
entries.learner_self_check: Have I shown earlier difficulties that explain why this last event mattered?

entries.title: in hot water
entries.meaning_or_strategy: In trouble or facing criticism or consequences for something.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: be/get in hot water (with someone).
entries.independent_illustration: Milo got in hot water with the club organiser after changing the schedule without asking.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The person is in a difficult social situation, not literally in heated water.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: The degree of trouble depends on context; it does not necessarily imply legal trouble or danger.
entries.learner_self_check: Can I replace it with in trouble naturally, and is the tone informal enough?

entries.title: distinguish the main claim from an example
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Identify what a paragraph mainly asserts and what merely illustrates it; this is more specific than the existing pilot reminder REF-TIP-01 gist before detail.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: (1) Ask what all sentences contribute to. (2) Identify the broader claim. (3) Label one supporting example. (4) Check that the claim does not overstate the paragraph.
entries.independent_illustration: Small public gardens benefit city insects. For example, the new flower beds outside the library attract bees. The first sentence makes the broad claim; the second gives one example.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: The mention of bees is evidence or illustration of a broader point, not necessarily the whole main idea.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Not every paragraph begins with its main idea; in narrative writing, the central point may be implied.
entries.learner_self_check: Does my summary include the broader idea without being just a copy of the bee example?

entries.title: follow contrast and concession in a text
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Notice when a writer introduces a competing fact or changes the expected direction of an argument.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: Underline a cue (but, however, although), identify both ideas, then explain which limitation or change the cue signals.
entries.independent_illustration: Although the path was longer, it had fewer steep steps. The second clause presents a benefit that qualifies the disadvantage in the first.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Knowing the word although is not enough; the reader must understand the relationship between the two parts.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Discourse markers can be used in nuanced ways. The presence of however alone does not prove the author's final opinion.
entries.learner_self_check: Can I state both sides in my own words, including what is being conceded?

entries.title: separate event order from cause
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Avoid assuming that the event reported first caused the event reported next.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: (1) Mark sequence words (then, after). (2) Look for explicit cause cues (because, therefore) or independent evidence. (3) If none exists, retain uncertainty.
entries.independent_illustration: It rained during the afternoon. That evening, the science fair was postponed. The order is clear; the short text does not explicitly establish why the fair was postponed.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: A plausible link between rain and postponement is not the same as a stated or well-supported cause.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Writers sometimes imply causal links without using because. Do not deny evidence-based inference merely because a signal word is missing.
entries.learner_self_check: Which exact words or facts support the cause I am claiming?

entries.title: resolve reference words in context
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Work out what it, they, this, those or similar references point to in a passage.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: Look back to nearby candidates, check number and meaning, then reread the sentence with the likely noun substituted.
entries.independent_illustration: Asha placed the new lens in a box because it was fragile. Here it most naturally refers to the lens rather than the box, given the reason supplied.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Grammar may narrow candidates, but meaning and context often settle the reference.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Some pronoun references genuinely remain ambiguous; do not claim certainty when two readings are plausible.
entries.learner_self_check: Does substituting my chosen noun preserve the sentence's sense?

entries.title: make a limited inference from text evidence
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Infer what is reasonably supported but not directly stated; this operationalises, rather than replaces, pilot REF-TIP-02 evidence vs assumption.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: Separate (1) direct statement, (2) justified implication, and (3) attractive but unsupported guess; name at least one clue for the implication.
entries.independent_illustration: The café chairs were stacked and the sign on the door read “Back at eight tomorrow.” The café is probably closed now; the micro-text does not prove the owner is on holiday.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: “Closed now” is supported by several details; “on holiday” adds a story with no text evidence.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Inference can remain probabilistic. An answer should not be described as definitely true when the clues allow alternatives.
entries.learner_self_check: Which detail supports my inference, and what stronger claim have I deliberately avoided?

entries.title: decide the listening purpose before play
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Decide whether the task asks about overall situation, a detail, an intention or a change; listen with a clear purpose rather than trying to memorise all sounds.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: (1) Read the legitimate task instructions. (2) Identify what type of information is needed. (3) Play the verified audio. (4) Refine attention on a later listen if necessary.
entries.independent_illustration: Fictional teaching scenario: A short museum announcement may require identifying where to meet, rather than memorising every item described in the announcement.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Purposeful attention reduces overload; it does not guarantee a correct answer.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Do not reveal a current lesson's hidden audio script, answer key, or any content clue masquerading as “help”. This description is not hearing evidence.
entries.learner_self_check: Before playing, can I say what kind of information I need without guessing the answer?

entries.title: use the first listen for gist
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Identify the main situation or topic before chasing every word.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: After a genuine first listen, ask who is involved, what situation is occurring and the broad reason for the message; listen again for unresolved details as appropriate.
entries.independent_illustration: Fictional teaching scenario: During a short club announcement, a learner first recognises that a meeting arrangement is being discussed, without yet knowing its exact time.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Gist is an overall understanding; one isolated familiar word may be misleading.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: This does not impose a compulsory number of plays or award Listening evidence without real playable audio and its playback guard.
entries.learner_self_check: Can I express the situation in one short phrase while keeping unknown details as unknown?

entries.title: track a change of plan or contrast
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Detect when a speaker corrects an earlier choice or changes direction.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: When genuine audio contains contrast language (but, instead, actually, in the end), notice the later relevant information and check whether it revises what came before.
entries.independent_illustration: Invented post-submit teaching illustration, not an active transcript: “We considered the garden, but we chose the library hall in the end.” The final location is the hall in this fictional example.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: A first-mentioned option may be rejected; focus on what the message finally commits to, where that is the task's purpose.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: This is a generic explanation only. Never display a current graded lesson's alternative choices or correct answer before submission; an isolated word such as but is not a complete answer.
entries.learner_self_check: In a fresh audio clip, can I distinguish an initial possibility from the final decision?

entries.title: check numbers, time and corrected details
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Distinguish a number or time actually confirmed by a speaker from one that was replaced or misheard.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: On verified audio, listen for the relevant quantity/unit, note whether the speaker corrects it, and make an additional focused listen where allowed.
entries.independent_illustration: Invented post-submit teaching illustration: A fictional speaker corrects “Thursday afternoon” to “Friday morning”; the correction, rather than the first time phrase, matters in that example.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: An early date can be a false lead when the speaker explicitly revises it.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: Accent, speech rate and numbers can be challenging; a written illustration cannot substitute for heard verification. Do not expose answer-specific timestamps or actual hidden scripts before a graded submission.
entries.learner_self_check: Did I hear a revision, and did I keep track of whether the unit was a date, time, amount or location?

entries.title: replay strategically and use transcripts only when allowed
entries.meaning_or_strategy: Use additional listens to resolve a concrete uncertainty; use a transcript as post-submit feedback, not a pre-answer shortcut.
entries.pattern_or_procedure: (1) Identify the uncertain part after first listening. (2) Replay the available verified audio as the lesson permits. (3) Answer from actual hearing. (4) Review a transcript only after submission where the lesson releases it, checking how the missed wording sounds.
entries.independent_illustration: Fictional teaching scenario: A learner is confident about a message's topic but unsure about its meeting place; the next listen focuses on location words, not every sentence.
entries.contrast_or_reasoning: Targeted replay can be more useful than unfocused repeated playback. Reading a transcript beforehand would instead test reading, not listening.
entries.watch_out_or_limits: No fixed number of plays proves proficiency. The supported audio player must still verify full playback for the relevant attempt; missing or invalid audio means UNASSESSED for Listening. Do not invent a transcript-release button if the runtime does not have one.
entries.learner_self_check: What specific uncertainty should my next real listen resolve?
